newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordanians end protest at Israel fair, call strike.
newsitem.headline: Jordanians end protest at Israel fair, call strike.

text.p: Jordan's professional unions called a three-day strike starting on Thursday to protest against the holding of the first Israeli trade fair in the kingdom.
The announcement of the strike call by unions boasting 100,000 members came as more than 1,000 Jordanians ended their protest outside the fair at the end of Wednesday's first day of the exhibition.
Former prime minister and intelligence chief Ahmed Obeidat, who led the campaign, said organisers believed it was in the "national interest" to end the protests near the fair.
"The protest has ended and there could not have been a clearer and greater expression of Jordanians' rejection of this fair and normalisation with Israel," Obeidat told Reuters.
Sources among the organisers said there were fears of clashes with police if protests continued until the fair ends on Saturday.
However, Obeidat said about a dozen professional unions with over 100,000 members decided to call a three-day work stoppage starting on Thursday for the duration of the exhibition.
The trade fair, delayed for a few hours, opened on Wednesday behind heavy police protection. Seventy Israeli companies and over 150 Israeli businessmen attended.

"The opposition to the exhibition is being used as an excuse to express dissatisfaction with the peace process, Jordan's peace treaty with Israel and even the existence of the state of Israel," Israeli ambassador to Jordan, Shimon Shamir, told reporters at the opening ceremony.

The protests are organised by a "national committee" that represents a broad coalition of 19 parties, 18 unions and business lobbies. It reflects anti-Israeli feelings among many Jordanians who still shun contacts despite a 1994 peace treaty that ended a 46-year state of war.
Scores of riot police blocked protesters who tried to reach the site hours before the trade fair was to open, witnesses said. Three rows of police sealed off the main street leading to the fair.
Demonstrators had chanted Islam's rallying cry of "Allahu Akbar" (God is Greatest) and "Jordan's land is Arab not Zionist".
Some police officers tore banners and a few protesters were bruised in minor scuffles, witnesses said. An armoured police vehicle splashed coloured water over some protesters.
Organisers said police prevented their supporters in cities across the country from setting off in buses organised to bring demonstrators to Amman.
Laith Shubailat, an opposition activist who heads the Islamist-dominated Jordan Engineers Association, accused King Hussein's government of "becoming an agent of Zionism to Judaise Jordan."
